newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Korean Air crash rate relatively high.
newsitem.headline: Korean Air crash rate relatively high.

text.p: The crash of a Korean Air Lines (KAL) jumbo jet in Guam on Wednesday was the airline's first since 1989, but the company's accident rate is seen as relatively high.

Marty Salfen, senior vice president of the International Airline Passengers Association, said KAL had an accident rate of 1.91 per million departures over the past 10 years against the worldwide rate of 0.581 per million.

KAL itself gives no information on its accident rate. Salfen's figure does not include the loss of KAL flight 007, a Boeing 747 that strayed into Soviet airspace in 1983 and was shot down. All 269 people aboard died.

Hours after the Guam crash a KAL Airbus A300 en route to Seoul from Osaka returned to Kansai airport in western Japan when it experienced engine trouble shortly after takeoff, an official of the airline said.
Disaster last hit KAL on July 27, 1989, when a KAL DC-10 jet carrying 199 people crashed near fog-bound Tripoli airport, killing 80 people, including several on the ground, and injuring 70.

The South Korean government ruled the cockpit crew of the Tripoli flight had committed a "preposterous error" and had ignored three warnings before the pilot crash-landed the KAL jet. The pilot was jailed for two years.
An analyst with a foreign securities house who asked not to be identified said Wednesday's crash on Guam, with more than 200 feared dead, would damage the airline's credibility and image.
"The accident is a very negative factor. Korean Air is known as one of the riskier airlines to foreign passengers, in particular, who are keen on safety."
Park Yoo-kyung, an airline analyst at ING-Barings, said she worried about long-term side-effects of the crash.
"It will definitely hurt Korean Air's image," Park said.
A KAL spokesman said the airline's reputation had suffered unfairly.
"It's unfair because past crashes originated from political issues," said Jeong Jin-wook, a KAL spokesman.
Of KAL's 10 major civilian aviation incidents since 1969, five were related to North Korea terrorism or violations of Soviet Union airspace.
The cause of the Guam crash has not been determined but analysts said Korean passengers would stick with KAL.
"Korean tourists are not likely to switch to foreign airlines. They prefer the nation's airlines due to language and more familiar services," said Choi Young-ho, analyst at Ssangyong Securities.
KAL is expected next week to announce huge losses for the first half of calendar 1997, but analysts said those losses should narrow for the whole year despite Wednesday's crash.

Analysts forecast first-half losses for the company of 150 billion won ($168.5 million) to 220 billion won against a 253.8 billion loss during the same period a year earlier. The company experienced substantial foreign currency translation losses, they said.
Korean Air is an affiliate of South Korea's seventh largest conglomerate, Hanjin Group.
Analysts said full-year losses were expected to decline to 100-180 billion won from a 246 billion loss a year ago on an improved national economy and increased domestic air fares.

South Korea's last major civilian aviation disaster occurred on July 26, 1993, when a Boeing 737-500 operated by KAL rival Asiana Airlines slammed into a cliff near the southwest Korean city of Mokpo, killing 66 of the 110 passengers and crew aboard.
The Asiana plane crashed after the pilot had tried to land three times in driving wind and rain.
(Conversion $1 = 890.00 won)
